title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
problem_statement: Multi-task learning frequently suffers from negative transfer and optimization difficulties caused by conflicting gradients across tasks; existing gradient manipulation methods alter gradients after computation but fail to prevent the occurrence of conflicting gradients in shared parameters.
domain: Multi-Task Learning — Multi-Task Computer Vision (Multi-Fashion+MNIST, CelebA, CityScapes, NYUv2, and PASCAL-Context)
theoretical_framework: First-order Taylor expansion and layer-wise gradient conflict analysis in multi-task optimization; Theorem 4.1 proves that when task gradients satisfy the cosine projection condition cos(φ_ij^(k)) ||g_i^(k)|| < ||g_j^(k)|| across selected conflict layers, an update under Recon achieves strictly lower multi-task loss than an update under the standard shared architecture for sufficiently small learning rates.
methodology: Recon (Removing Layer-wise Conflicting Gradients) addresses task conflicts at the architectural level. In the search phase, the network is trained for initial iterations (e.g., the first 25% of training epochs) using joint training or gradient manipulation while computing layer-wise S-conflict scores s^(k) (the frequency with which pairwise cosine similarities between task gradients fall below severity threshold S). In the modification phase, the top-K shared layers exhibiting the highest conflict scores are turned into task-specific layers, and the modified network architecture is retrained from scratch.
datasets: Multi-Fashion+MNIST (two-task image classification benchmark combining FashionMNIST and MNIST items)
CityScapes (urban scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation)
NYUv2 (indoor scene understanding benchmark evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction)
PASCAL-Context (multi-task dense visual perception benchmark evaluated on semantic segmentation, human parts segmentation, saliency estimation, surface normal estimation, and edge detection)
CelebA (large-scale facial attribute benchmark containing 40 binary classification tasks)

metrics: Mean classification error (%) across 40 attribute prediction tasks on CelebA
Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and absolute error (Abs Err) for CityScapes semantic segmentation and depth estimation

Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU), pixel accuracy (Pix Acc), absolute error (Abs Err), relative error (Rel Err), mean angle distance, median angle distance, and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for NYUv2

Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic and human parts segmentation, root mean square error (RMSE) for surface normal estimation, and mean optimal dataset scale F-score (mODS) for edge detection and saliency on PASCAL-Context
Average relative task improvement (Δm%) with respect to single-task learning baselines across all tasks
Model size in megabytes (#P in MB) and parameter increase percentage
Percentage reduction of conflicting gradients (cos φ_ij < S)
baselines: Joint training (equal loss weights with shared backbone)
Projecting Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad; Yu et al., 2020)
Gradient Sign Dropout (GradDrop; Chen et al., 2020)
Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent (CAGrad; Liu et al., 2021a)
Branched Multi-Task Architecture Search (BMTAS; Bruggemann et al., 2020)
Random Layer Selection (RSL) and Random Parameter Selection (RSP) ablation baselines
First K layers (FSK) and Last K layers (LSK) selection baselines
architectures: ResNet18 backbone for Multi-Fashion+MNIST and CelebA
SegNet encoder-decoder architecture with split convolutional decoders for CityScapes
Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with SegNet backbone for NYUv2
MobileNetV2 with Reduced ASPP (R-ASPP) backbone pre-trained on ImageNet for PASCAL-Context
SegNet backbone for NYUv2 cross-architecture transfer experiments
MTAN backbone for CityScapes cross-architecture transfer experiments

key_findings: Recon consistently improves the multi-task learning performance of all evaluated base models, including joint training, gradient manipulation methods (MGDA, PCGrad, GradDrop, CAGrad, RotoGrad), and branched architecture search methods (BMTAS, MMoE), across all 5 benchmark datasets.

Modifying a small proportion of shared parameters into task-specific parameters yields substantial performance gains; Recon converts only 1.42% of parameters on Multi-Fashion+MNIST, 1.46% on CelebA, 12.77% on CityScapes, 0.26% on NYUv2, and 9.80% on PASCAL-Context, with overall model size increasing by only 0.52% to 57.25%.

Recon reduces severe conflicting gradients (cos φ_ij ∈ (−0.01, −1.0]) in remaining shared parameters by 67% to 79% on Multi-Fashion+MNIST, and over 50% across CityScapes, NYUv2, and PASCAL-Context, whereas existing gradient manipulation methods only slightly decrease or sometimes increase gradient conflicts.

Recon combined with gradient manipulation methods (such as CAGrad w/ Recon) achieves superior performance compared to branched architecture search methods (BMTAS) while utilizing substantially fewer parameters.

Identified conflict layers are highly stable across training stages (early 25% versus later iterations), across different multi-task optimization algorithms, and transfer effectively across datasets sharing the same backbone architecture (e.g., 100% layer overlap between Multi-Fashion+MNIST and CelebA on ResNet18; 95% layer overlap between NYUv2 and CityScapes on SegNet).

Ablation experiments confirm that targeted selection of top conflict layers is essential: random layer selection (RSL), random parameter selection (RSP), first-K layer selection (FSK), and last-K layer selection (LSK) all incur significant performance drops relative to Recon.

Theorem 4.1 mathematically proves that under the cosine projection condition, a single gradient update under Recon achieves strictly lower multi-task loss than an update under the fully shared network.
scope_and_delimitations: Evaluates multi-task convolutional architectures (ResNet18, SegNet, MTAN, MobileNetV2) exclusively across visual image classification and dense visual perception datasets.

Requires a two-stage training workflow: an initial search phase (e.g., the first 25% of training epochs) to compute pairwise layer-wise conflict scores, followed by training the modified network from scratch.
Requires tuning two discrete hyperparameters per architecture: the conflict severity threshold S ∈ (−1, 0] and the number of converted task-specific layers K.
Focuses on hard parameter sharing architectures converted via layer duplication rather than soft modular routing or dynamic weight generation.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: The results in Fig. [11](#page-19-0) show that Recon is as fast as other gradient manipulation methods such as CAGrad [\(Liu et al., 2021a\)](#page-10-5) and Graddrop [\(Chen et al., 2020\)](#page-9-3), but much slower than joint-training especially when the number of tasks is large, which is natural since Recon needs to compute pariwise cosine similarity of task gradients. However, since Recon only needs to search for the conflict layers once for a given network architecture, as discussed above, the running time is not a problem.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that Recon is much slower than joint training during the conflict score computation phase when the number of tasks is large because computing pairwise cosine similarities of task gradients scales quadratically with the task count; additionally, the approach requires two hyperparameters (conflict severity S and number of selected layers K) which are sensitive to tune, and computing conflict scores during early iterations exhibits slight noise compared to later iterations.

generalizability_gap: Recon was evaluated exclusively on computer vision classification and dense prediction tasks with convolutional backbones; the authors did not test the method on natural language processing tasks, transformer architectures, code-switched text, reinforcement learning domains, or multi-modal settings.
methodological_gap: Recon relies on discrete layer-level duplication rather than soft parameter sharing, fine-grained sub-layer modularization, or automated continuous architecture search; furthermore, pairwise conflict score computation scales quadratically with the number of tasks O(T^2), which introduces computational overhead for large task sets.
future_work: Extending layer-wise gradient conflict analysis to broader network families including Transformer-based architectures and recurrent models.
Applying Recon to non-vision modalities such as natural language processing, speech recognition, and multi-task reinforcement learning.
Developing adaptive or automated selection mechanisms for hyperparameters K (number of conflict layers) and S (conflict severity threshold) to eliminate manual tuning.
Investigating hybrid architectures combining layer-wise conflict isolation with dynamic routing or soft parameter sharing.
